title: A finite-type stalk isomorphism over a reduced finite-component target spreads to an open immersion
statement: Let $g:Y\to X$ be a finite-type morphism of schemes [def-pc-scheme, def-weil-finite-type-morphism]. Suppose $X$ is reduced [def-pc-reduced-scheme] and has finitely many irreducible components [def-weil-irreducible-components]. Let $y\in Y$, put $x=g(y)$, and assume that the induced map of local rings $\mathcal O_{X,x}\to\mathcal O_{Y,y}$ [def-weil-pbc-module-stalk] is an isomorphism. Then there exists an open neighbourhood $V\subseteq Y$ of $y$ such that $g|_V:V\to X$ is an open immersion [def-weil-open-immersion]. No finite-presentation, Noetherian, or reduced-source hypothesis is imposed.

source.place: Tag 09NH, label lemma-local-isomorphism, statement and proof immediately preceding Tag 09NI.

proof.text: Remove from $X$ the union of its finitely many irreducible components not containing $x$, obtaining an open $X_0$ containing $x$. Choose an affine open $U=\operatorname{Spec}A\subseteq X_0$ containing $x$. By the definition of locally finite type, choose a member $W=\operatorname{Spec}B$ of the finite-type affine cover of $g^{-1}(U)$ containing $y$, with $B$ a finitely generated $A$-algebra. Write $\varphi:A\to B$ for the restricted map on coordinate rings. The ring $A$ is reduced. Every irreducible component $D$ of $U$ is $C\cap U$ for an irreducible component $C$ of $X$: indeed the components-cover lemma puts the irreducible subset $D$ in some $C$, and the components-open-injection lemma makes $C\cap U$ a component of $U$, so maximality gives equality. Such a $C$ meets $X_0$, hence contains $x$. Thus every component of $\operatorname{Spec}A$ contains $x$. By the spectrum components/minimal-primes correspondence, every minimal prime of $A$ is contained in the prime $\mathfrak p$ corresponding to $x$.

Let $\mathfrak q\subset B$ correspond to $y$. The affine spectrum dictionary gives $\mathfrak p=\varphi^{-1}(\mathfrak q)$. The affine-open stalk-localization theorem identifies the ambient stalks at $x,y$ with $A_{\mathfrak p},B_{\mathfrak q}$, and the spectrum-map stalk formula identifies the induced map with $a/s\mapsto\varphi(a)/\varphi(s)$. Thus the hypothesis says that this particular map $\alpha:A_{\mathfrak p}\to B_{\mathfrak q}$ is an isomorphism.

The map $A\to A_{\mathfrak p}$ is injective. In fact, if $a/1=0$, the fraction equivalence relation supplies $s\notin\mathfrak p$ with $sa=0$. Every minimal prime $\mathfrak r$ is contained in $\mathfrak p$, so $s\notin\mathfrak r$ and primality gives $a\in\mathfrak r$. Every prime contains a minimal prime, so $a$ lies in every prime. The radical/intersection formula with the zero ideal implies that $a$ is nilpotent, hence zero since $A$ is reduced.

Choose algebra generators $b_1,\ldots,b_r$ of $B$ over $A$. Represent each $\alpha^{-1}(b_i/1)$ by a fraction $c_i/s_i$ in $A_{\mathfrak p}$. Set $f=\prod_i s_i
otin\mathfrak p$ and $a_i=c_i\prod_{j
e i}s_j$, so $b_i/1=\varphi(a_i)/\varphi(f)$ in $B_{\mathfrak q}$. The zero-fraction criterion supplies $g_i
otin\mathfrak q$ with $g_i(\varphi(f)b_i-\varphi(a_i))=0$ in $B$. Set $h=\prod_i g_i
otin\mathfrak q$; then $h(\varphi(f)b_i-\varphi(a_i))=0$ for every $i$. Empty products are $1$, so the construction also covers $r=0$.

Put $C=B_{\varphi(f)h}$. In $C$ both $\varphi(f)$ and $h$ are units, so the localization universal property gives $\beta:A_f\to C$ and the equations above give $b_i=\beta(a_i/f)$. Since the $b_i$ generate $B$, its entire image in $C$, in particular the image of $h$, lies in $\beta(A_f)$. Choose $f'\in A$ and $N\geq0$ with $\beta(f'/f^N)=h$. The natural map $C\to B_{\mathfrak q}$ exists because $\varphi(f)h\notin\mathfrak q$. In $B_{\mathfrak q}$, the image of $f'$ is $\varphi(f)^N h$, a unit. Under the isomorphism $\alpha$ this says $f'/1$ is a unit in the local ring $A_{\mathfrak p}$, whose maximal ideal is $\mathfrak pA_{\mathfrak p}$; hence $f'\notin\mathfrak p$.

The images of $f$ and $f'$ are units in $C$, so the universal property extends $\varphi$ to $\gamma:A_{ff'}\to C$. This map is surjective: its image contains $B$ by the generator equations, contains $\varphi(f)^{-1}$, and contains $h^{-1}$ because $h=f'/f^N$ and thus $h^{-1}=f^N/f'$ in $C$; every element of $C$ is $b/(\varphi(f)h)^k$. It is injective as well: its composite with $C\to B_{\mathfrak q}$ equals $A_{ff'}\to A_{\mathfrak p}\xrightarrow{\alpha}B_{\mathfrak q}$, by the fraction formula. If $a/(ff')^k$ vanishes under this composite then $a/1=0$ in $A_{\mathfrak p}$, whence $a=0$ by step 3. Therefore $\gamma$ is an isomorphism.

By the principal-localization open-immersion theorem, $V=D_B(\varphi(f)h)\subseteq W$ is the open subscheme $\operatorname{Spec}C$ and $D_A(ff')\subseteq U$ is $\operatorname{Spec}A_{ff'}$. The point $y$ belongs to $V$, since $\varphi(f)h\notin\mathfrak q$. Contravariant functoriality of spectrum takes the isomorphism $\gamma$ to an isomorphism $V\cong D_A(ff')$ over $U$. Consequently the original $g|_V$ identifies $V$ with this open subscheme of $U$, hence with an open subscheme of $X$. This is an open immersion by definition, as required.
